messages.author: c6308b8a6aace4ef
messages.subject: interpretation of centroid size
parts: Is centroid size an absolute measure of size? My data is 3D bill shape and I want to know if centroid size is a measure of absolute bill size or bill size relative to body size. I'm hoping centroid size is a measure of the latter to account for instances where small birds have big bills relative to their body size (like some of the Darwin's finches for example). If not, how could I get this metric?

messages.author: baf6eb7bae06984d
messages.subject: Re: interpretation of centroid size
parts:
Centroid size is not an absolute measure of size at all. It will be entirely dependent on the landmarks you choose to represent the structure, and it will change accordingly.

How well it correlates with the body size or the relative to body size is something you need to investigate. There is no definitive answer for that.

You might start with a simple correlation or a regression analysis.

messages.author: baf6eb7bae06984d
messages.subject: Re: interpretation of centroid size
parts:
It is somewhat unclear to me what you want to do. Are you interested in studying the allometric scaling of bill size with respect to body size? And also what is your measure of body size (weight?, volume? cranio-caudal length?, some sort of surface area?). The dimensions of  the input data will determine how you interpret the coefficients from that regression, i.e., whether your hard-seed eating groups have bills indeed relatively big for their body size.

If your goal is to study allometric relationship between bill shape and bill size, then you would generally do an regression of log(centroid size) on procrustes coordinates. If you want to study the shape patterns in groups after that relationship is accounted for then you would use the residuals from that regression. procD.lm() is the function in the geomorph to do that. Alternatively for the shape allometry model, as the size measure you can opt to use directly the body size, as oppose the centroid size of your bill landmarks.

messages.author: baf6eb7bae06984d
messages.subject: Re: interpretation of centroid size
parts:
So in the realm of traditional morphometrics, it is somewhat unusual to use centroid size as a measure of size. Because unlike physical traits like weight, height, length, cross-section, volume, centroid size is not just the property of an individual, but also depends on landmarks chosen. As such, while it can have a unit like mm, it is not a fixed value and will only exist in the context of that analysis. I don't know how many landmarks you have, but take randomly half of them out and recalculate the centroid size, and repeat a few times, and you will see the value, and possibly the relationship, change.

You said you have 3D data. Perhaps calculating volumes of bill, or surface areas might be a more prudent approach?

Regardless, what you describe seems correct -with the caveat above- to me.
